The longest carbon chain that contains the double bond runs through the methyl group written below the carbon bearing bromine, so it is a **five** carbon chain: \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=C(CH_3)-CHBr-CH_3}\).

Numbering from the left gives the double bond locant 2; numbering from the right would give it 3, so the chain is numbered from the left. The bromine is then on carbon 4 and the methyl branch on carbon 3.

IUPAC name: **4-bromo-3-methylpent-2-ene**.

The longest chain has five carbons, so the parent is pentane. Numbering from the left puts chlorine on carbon 2 and the methyl branch on carbon 3, giving the locant set \(\{2,3\}\); numbering from the right would give \(\{3,4\}\), which is higher. Chloro is cited before methyl because substituent prefixes are listed alphabetically.

IUPAC name: **2-chloro-3-methylpentane**.

The ring is saturated, so the parent hydrocarbon is cyclohexane. It carries a chlorine atom on one carbon and an ethyl group on the carbon directly opposite, that is, on carbon 4 when the ring is numbered starting from the substituted carbon.

Of the two substituents, chloro comes first alphabetically, so it is given the lower locant.

IUPAC name: **1-chloro-4-ethylcyclohexane**.

The ring is aromatic, so the parent is benzene. It carries two chlorine atoms para to each other and a methyl group on a carbon adjacent to one of them.

Numbering must give the lowest set of locants. Starting at the chlorine that is next to the methyl group and counting towards the methyl group gives \(\{1,2,4\}\) (chlorines at 1 and 4, methyl at 2); every other way of numbering gives a higher set such as \(\{1,3,4\}\) or \(\{1,4,5\}\).

IUPAC name: **1,4-dichloro-2-methylbenzene** (also written as 2,5-dichlorotoluene).

This is the **Finkelstein reaction** (halogen exchange, section 10.3.3). Sodium iodide is soluble in dry acetone while sodium chloride is not, so \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) precipitates and drives the equilibrium to the right.

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{acetone}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2I} + \mathrm{NaCl} \downarrow\)

Structure of the major product: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2I}\)

IUPAC name: **1-iodo-2-methylpropane**.

This is the **Swartz reaction**: an alkyl bromide (or chloride) heated with a metallic fluoride such as \(\mathrm{SbF_3}\) exchanges its halogen for fluorine, which is the practical way of making an alkyl fluoride.

\(3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br} + \mathrm{SbF_3} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2F} + \mathrm{SbBr_3}\)

Structure of the major product: \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-F}\)

IUPAC name: **fluoroethane**.

Peroxide is present and the reagent is \(\mathrm{HBr}\), so the peroxide (Kharasch) effect operates and the addition is **anti-Markownikov**: bromine adds to the terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) of the double bond and hydrogen to the other doubly bonded carbon.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{HBr} \xrightarrow{\text{peroxide}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)

Structure of the major product: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)

IUPAC name: **1-bromo-3-methylbutane**.

Thionyl chloride replaces the hydroxyl group of an alcohol by chlorine (section 10.3.1, method c). It is the preferred route because both by-products, \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\), are gases and escape, so no effort is needed to separate them.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-OH} + \mathrm{SOCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_{11}-Cl} + \mathrm{SO_2} \uparrow + \mathrm{HCl} \uparrow\)

Structure of the major product: a cyclohexane ring carrying one chlorine atom, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}Cl}\)

IUPAC name: **chlorocyclohexane**.

In the **dark** and in the presence of a halogen carrier such as \(\mathrm{Fe}\) (or \(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\)), chlorine attacks the **ring** rather than the side chain. The methyl group is an ortho/para directing group, so chlorine enters at the position next to it or opposite to it.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Fe}]{\text{dark}} \mathrm{Cl-C_6H_4-CH_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Both the ortho and the para product are formed. The **para** isomer is the major product, because the position opposite the methyl group is free of the steric crowding that hinders attack next to it.

Structure of the major product: a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a chlorine atom on opposite carbons.

IUPAC name: **1-chloro-4-methylbenzene** (p-chlorotoluene).

[Textbook misprint: alternative d is printed as \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_3-CH_3}\), in which the third carbon is written \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) in the middle of a chain and so would carry five bonds. It is transcribed exactly as printed; the intended structure is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3}\), 2-methylbutane. The answer is unaffected, because 2-methylbutane has no carbon bonded to four different groups and so is achiral on either reading.]

A molecule is chiral when it contains a carbon bonded to four different groups (section 10.5.1). Testing each compound:

**a. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CH_3}\) (butan-2-ol)** — carbon 2 carries \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{OH}\), four different groups. It **is chiral**.

b. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CHBr-CH_2-CH_3}\) (3-bromopentane) — carbon 3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so it is not a chiral carbon. Not chiral.

c. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2Br}\) (1-bromobutane) — the carbon bearing bromine also carries two hydrogens. Not chiral.

d. The branched compound as printed has no carbon carrying four different groups; its central carbon bears two methyl groups. Not chiral.

So only compound **a** is a chiral molecule.

The \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) transition state is pentacoordinate and therefore crowded, so the rate falls as the carbon under attack becomes more substituted: primary > secondary > tertiary (section 10.6.4).

In \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-CH_2Cl}\) the chlorine sits on a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group, that is, on a **primary** carbon, and the bulky ring is one bond further away from the site of attack. In \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-Cl}\) the chlorine is on a ring carbon that is joined to two other ring carbons, so it is a **secondary** carbon and the two neighbouring \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) groups of the ring crowd the transition state.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-CH_2Cl}\), the primary halide, therefore undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) faster.

Both compounds are primary halides with the same carbon skeleton, so the crowding at the reacting carbon is identical and the difference must lie in the halogen.

The C-I bond is longer and weaker than the C-Cl bond, and iodide is a larger, more polarisable ion that carries its negative charge better, so it is a much better leaving group. This is why the reactivity of alkyl halides runs \(\mathrm{R-I} > \mathrm{R-Br} > \mathrm{R-Cl}\) (section 10.6.2).

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2I}\) therefore undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) faster.

**Step 1.** Peroxide is present and the reagent is \(\mathrm{HBr}\), so the addition is anti-Markownikov and bromine goes to the terminal carbon.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)

**A = 1-bromopropane**

**Step 2.** Alcoholic KOH brings about dehydrohalogenation (section 10.6.5): a \(\beta\)-hydrogen and the halogen are eliminated to give an alkene.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2}\)

**B = propene (prop-1-ene)**, the only alkene possible here since there is just one kind of \(\beta\)-hydrogen.

**Step 1.** Red phosphorus and bromine generate phosphorus tribromide in the reaction mixture, and \(\mathrm{PBr_3}\) replaces the hydroxyl group of the alcohol by bromine (section 10.3.1, method b).

\(3\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} + \mathrm{PBr_3} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)

**A = 2-bromopropane**

**Step 2.** Moist silver oxide supplies hydroxide ion, which substitutes the bromine and gives back the alcohol.

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3} + \mathrm{Ag_2O} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} + 2\,\mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)

**B = propan-2-ol** (isopropyl alcohol).

[Note: it is the water that decides this. **Dry** silver oxide would instead give the ether, di-isopropyl ether.]

Sodium in dry ether brings about the **Wurtz reaction**: two molecules of the alkyl halide are coupled, giving an alkane with twice the number of carbon atoms (section 10.6, b).

\(2\,\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CH_2Cl} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CH_2-CH_2-C(CH_3)_3} + 2\,\mathrm{NaCl}\)

**A** is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CH_2-CH_2-C(CH_3)_3}\), that is, **2,2,5,5-tetramethylhexane**.

Magnesium in dry ether inserts into the carbon-halogen bond to give a Grignard reagent, and the chapter notes that vinyl and aryl halides also form Grignard reagents.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} + \mathrm{Mg} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-MgCl}\)

**A = phenylmagnesium chloride**, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Mg-Cl}\).

The ether must be dry: a Grignard reagent is destroyed by water or by any compound with hydrogen attached to an electronegative element, which would convert it back to benzene.

The reagent is **sodium ethoxide, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5ONa}\)** (an alkoxide, \(\mathrm{NaOR'}\) in Table 10.3). The alkoxide ion acts as the nucleophile and displaces bromide; this is Williamson's ether synthesis.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{C_2H_5ONa} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{NaBr}\)

The reagent is **silver nitrite, \(\mathrm{AgNO_2}\)** (Table 10.3). With the silver salt the nitrogen atom of the ambident nitrite ion attacks the carbon, so a **nitroalkane** is obtained; with sodium nitrite the oxygen attacks instead and the product would be the alkyl nitrite.

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{AgNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NO_2} + \mathrm{AgCl} \downarrow\)

The reagent is **silver cyanide, \(\mathrm{AgCN}\)**, in alcohol (Table 10.3). With the silver salt the **nitrogen** of the ambident cyanide ion attacks the carbon and an isocyanide is formed; potassium cyanide would give the cyanide (nitrile) instead, because there the carbon attacks.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{AgCN} \xrightarrow{\text{alc.}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-N} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)

The reagent is **sodium metal in dry ether**. When only an aryl halide takes part, this coupling is called the **Fittig reaction** (section 10.6.1, a).

\(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5} + 2\,\mathrm{NaCl}\)

The product \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5}\) is biphenyl.

Two rules from section 10.4.2 settle this. (1) For the same halogen, the boiling point rises with the number of carbon atoms, because the molecule gets larger and the van der Waals forces get stronger. (2) For the same molecular formula, **branching lowers** the boiling point: a branched molecule is more nearly spherical, its surface area of contact is smaller and the van der Waals forces are weaker.

The four compounds fall into two pairs. Among the three-carbon pair, the branched 2-bromopropane boils below the straight-chain 1-bromopropane. Among the four-carbon pair, the branched 1-bromo-2-methylpropane boils below the straight-chain 1-bromobutane. Both three-carbon compounds boil below both four-carbon compounds.

Increasing order of boiling point:

**2-Bromopropane < 1-Bromopropane < 1-Bromo-2-methylpropane < 1-Bromobutane**

(that is, b < a < d < c).

The class of a halogen derivative is decided by the kind of carbon the halogen is joined to (section 10.1.1).

| Column I | matches | reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(X)-CH_3}\) | ii. alkyl halide | the halogen is on an \(sp^3\) carbon of a saturated chain |
| b. \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_2X}\) | iii. allyl halide | the halogen is on the \(sp^3\) carbon **next to** a doubly bonded carbon |
| c. \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-X}\) | i. vinyl halide | the halogen is joined **directly** to a doubly bonded \(sp^2\) carbon |

So the pairs are **a-ii, b-iii, c-i**. Entries iv (benzyl halide, the halogen on the carbon attached to a benzene ring) and v (aryl halide, the halogen on the ring itself) have no partner in Column I.

Two reasons are given in section 10.6.1 (b).

**i. Resonance effect.** One of the lone pairs on the halogen is in conjugation with the \(\pi\)-electrons of the ring, so resonance structures can be drawn in which the carbon-halogen bond is a double bond. The C-X bond therefore has partial double bond character and is shorter and stronger than in a haloalkane: the C-Cl bond length is **169 pm** in chlorobenzene against **178 pm** in an alkyl chloride. A shorter, stronger bond is harder to break.

**ii. \(sp^2\) hybrid state of carbon.** In a haloarene the carbon holding the halogen is \(sp^2\) hybridised, and an \(sp^2\) carbon is more electronegative than the \(sp^3\) carbon of a haloalkane, so it holds the shared electrons more tightly and shortens the bond further.

Both substitution routes are also blocked: the phenyl cation formed on self-ionisation is not stabilised by resonance, which rules out \(\mathrm{S_N1}\), and backside attack by the nucleophile is blocked by the aromatic ring, which rules out \(\mathrm{S_N2}\).

Hence haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes.

For a substance to dissolve in water, the new solute-water attractions must make up for the water-water hydrogen bonds that have to be broken.

Alkyl halides are only **moderately** polar, and — as section 10.4.3 states — they **cannot form hydrogen bonds with water**, because they have no hydrogen attached to a strongly electronegative atom and the halogen is held in a covalent bond. The weak dipole-dipole attraction they can offer a water molecule does not release enough energy to compensate for breaking the extensive hydrogen bonding of water.

So, although they are polar, alkyl halides remain immiscible with water. They dissolve readily in organic solvents, where only weak van der Waals forces have to be overcome.

In a Grignard reagent \(\mathrm{R-Mg-X}\) the carbon-magnesium bond is strongly polar: carbon pulls the electrons away from the electropositive magnesium, so the carbon carries a negative polarity and behaves like a carbanion.

Such a carbon is a powerful base and grabs a proton from **any** compound having hydrogen attached to an electronegative element — water, alcohols, ammonia, acids. The reagent is then destroyed, being converted into the corresponding hydrocarbon:

\(\mathrm{R-Mg-X} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-H} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\)

If even traces of moisture are present, the Grignard reagent is consumed in this way instead of taking part in the intended reaction, and the yield falls. Hence Grignard reactions must be carried out under strictly anhydrous conditions, which is why dry ether is used as the solvent.

As section 10.3.2 states, halogenation of alkanes is not suitable for preparing alkyl halides because **a mixture of mono and poly halogen compounds is formed**.

The reaction is a free radical chain: once a monohalide has been made, its remaining hydrogens are attacked just as readily, so di-, tri- and higher halogenated products accumulate alongside it. In addition, an alkane with more than one kind of hydrogen gives several isomeric monohalides, since the radical can be formed at any carbon.

The products have closely similar boiling points and are therefore troublesome to separate, and the yield of any one of them is poor. Cleaner routes — from alcohols with \(\mathrm{PX_3}\), \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) or \(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\), by addition of \(\mathrm{HX}\) to an alkene, or by halogen exchange — are used instead.

| Point of difference | \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism | \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Number of steps | Two steps: slow heterolysis of the C-X bond, then fast attack by the nucleophile | One single step; bond breaking and bond forming occur simultaneously |
| Intermediate / transition state | A planar **carbocation intermediate** is formed | No intermediate; a **pentacoordinate transition state** is formed |
| Rate law | rate \(= k\,[\text{substrate}]\) — first order | rate \(= k\,[\text{substrate}][\text{nucleophile}]\) — second order |
| Effect of nucleophile concentration | None, because the nucleophile is absent from the slow step | Rate is directly proportional to it |
| Molecularity of the slow step | Unimolecular (substitution nucleophilic unimolecular) | Bimolecular (substitution nucleophilic bimolecular) |
| Stereochemistry at a chiral carbon | Mainly **racemization**, since the flat carbocation is attacked from either face | **Inversion** of configuration (Walden inversion), since attack is from the side opposite the leaving group |
| Order of reactivity of alkyl halides | Tertiary > Secondary > Primary (carbocation stability) | Primary > Secondary > Tertiary (crowding in the transition state) |

In short, \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) is favoured by anything that stabilises a carbocation, and \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) by anything that keeps the reacting carbon uncrowded.

2-Chlorobutane is \(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{*}{C}HCl-CH_2-CH_3}\).

**The chiral carbon.** Carbon 2, marked with the asterisk, is bonded to four different groups: \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\). A carbon carrying four different groups is a chiral (asymmetric) carbon, so the molecule is chiral (section 10.5.1).

**Consequence.** A chiral molecule and its mirror image cannot be superimposed on each other, in the same way that a left hand cannot be placed on a right hand. 2-Chlorobutane therefore exists as **two** stereoisomers which are non-superimposable mirror images of each other; such isomers are called **enantiomers** (section 10.5.4, Fig. 10.1).

**Optical activity.** The two enantiomers rotate the plane of plane polarized light through **equal angles in opposite directions**. The one that rotates it to the right is dextrorotatory, written d- or (+); the one that rotates it to the left is laevorotatory, written l- or (-). Apart from the sign of rotation they have identical melting point, boiling point, density and chemical properties, and differ chemically only towards other optically active reagents.

**Racemic mixture.** An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic modification, written (dl) or (\(\pm\)). It is optically **inactive**, because the rotation due to one enantiomer is exactly cancelled by the equal and opposite rotation due to the other. This is what is obtained when 2-chlorobutane is prepared by an ordinary laboratory method, or when it is hydrolysed by the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) route.

The hydroxyl group has to end up on the **terminal** carbon, so the bromine must be placed there first, which needs the peroxide effect.

**Step 1** — anti-Markownikov addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) in the presence of peroxide:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)  (1-bromopropane)

**Step 2** — nucleophilic substitution by hydroxide (Table 10.3, entry 1):

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH\,(aq)}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2OH}\)  (propan-1-ol)

Note that \(\mathrm{HBr}\) without peroxide would follow Markownikov's rule and give 2-bromopropane, leading to propan-2-ol instead.

The hydroxyl group is not a leaving group, so it is first replaced by chlorine and the halide is then treated with cyanide.

**Step 1** — thionyl chloride converts the alcohol into the halide (section 10.3.1, method c):

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2OH} + \mathrm{SOCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{SO_2}\uparrow + \mathrm{HCl}\uparrow\)  (benzyl chloride)

**Step 2** — alcoholic KCN, where the **carbon** of the cyanide ion attacks (Table 10.3, entry 5):

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{KCN} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc.}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-C} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{N} + \mathrm{KCl}\)  (benzyl cyanide)

Silver cyanide must not be used here, as it would give the isocyanide instead.

Propanenitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2C} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{N}\), has three carbons: the two of the ethyl group plus the carbon of the cyanide, which is gained in the second step.

**Step 1** — replace the hydroxyl group by bromine (section 10.3.1, method b):

\(3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} + \mathrm{PBr_3} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br} + \mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)  (bromoethane)

**Step 2** — alcoholic KCN (Table 10.3, entry 5):

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br} + \mathrm{KCN} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc.}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{N} + \mathrm{KBr}\)  (propanenitrile)

n-Butyl iodide is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I}\), with the halogen on the **terminal** carbon, so the peroxide effect is needed in the first step; the iodide is then reached by halogen exchange, because direct addition of \(\mathrm{HI}\) does not show a peroxide effect.

**Step 1** — anti-Markownikov addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\):

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\)  (1-bromobutane)

**Step 2** — Finkelstein reaction, sodium iodide in dry acetone (section 10.3.3):

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br} + \mathrm{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{acetone}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I} + \mathrm{NaBr} \downarrow\)  (1-iodobutane)

The halogen has to be moved from carbon 2 to carbon 1, which is done by going through the alkene.

**Step 1** — dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH (section 10.6.5):

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHCl-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2}\)  (propene)

**Step 2** — anti-Markownikov addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) in the presence of peroxide, which places the halogen on the terminal carbon:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)  (1-bromopropane)

**Step 3** — hydrolysis with aqueous alkali (Table 10.3, entry 1):

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH\,(aq)}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2OH}\)  (propan-1-ol)

The bromine has to be moved from the tertiary carbon to a terminal carbon, and again the alkene is the bridge.

**Step 1** — dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH (section 10.6.5). A tertiary halide undergoes elimination readily:

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2}\)  (2-methylpropene)

**Step 2** — addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) **in the presence of peroxide**, so that the addition is anti-Markownikov and bromine goes to the terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2}\):

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2Br}\)  (isobutyl bromide, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane)

Without peroxide the second step would follow Markownikov's rule and simply return tert-butyl bromide.

A haloarene is normally very unwilling to undergo nucleophilic substitution, but the \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) group **para** to the halogen is strongly electron withdrawing and markedly activates the halogen towards substitution (section 10.6.1, b).

So p-nitrochlorobenzene can be hydrolysed with sodium hydroxide, though a high temperature is still needed, and the sodium salt formed is then acidified:

p-nitrochlorobenzene \(\xrightarrow[\text{(ii) } \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{\text{(i) NaOH, 433 K}}\) p-nitrophenol

For comparison, plain chlorobenzene needs about 623 K and 300 atm for the same conversion, which shows how much the para nitro group helps.

The nitro group has to end up on the terminal carbon, so the halogen is placed there first.

**Step 1** — anti-Markownikov addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) in the presence of peroxide:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)  (1-bromopropane)

**Step 2** — treatment with **silver nitrite** (Table 10.3, entry 8). With the silver salt the nitrogen of the nitrite ion attacks the carbon, so a nitroalkane is formed:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br} + \mathrm{AgNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NO_2} + \mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)  (1-nitropropane)

Sodium nitrite must not be used, as it would give propyl nitrite, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2-O-N{=}O}\), instead.

Work backwards from 'C'. The only **tertiary** alcohol with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\) is 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\).

Since 'C' comes from 'B' by hydrolysis with aqueous alkali, which replaces halogen by hydroxyl, 'B' must be the corresponding chloride, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Cl}\).

'B' in turn comes from adding \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to the hydrocarbon 'A', \(\mathrm{C_4H_8}\). For the chlorine to land on the carbon bearing three methyl groups, Markownikov's rule requires that carbon to be the more substituted one of the double bond, so 'A' is 2-methylpropene.

**A = 2-methylpropene**, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2}\)

**B = 2-chloro-2-methylpropane** (tert-butyl chloride), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Cl}\)

**C = 2-methylpropan-2-ol** (tert-butyl alcohol), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\)

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH\,(aq)}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\)

Both formulae check out: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2}\) is \(\mathrm{C_4H_8}\) and \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH}\) is \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\).

**A.** Alcoholic KOH removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen and the bromine (section 10.6.5). 2-Bromobutane has two different kinds of \(\beta\)-hydrogen, so both but-1-ene and but-2-ene are formed; by Saytzeff's rule the major product is the alkene with the greater number of alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons.

**A = but-2-ene**, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\)

**B.** Bromine adds across the double bond to give a vicinal dibromide.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3} + \mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CHBr-CH_3}\)

**B = 2,3-dibromobutane**

**C.** Sodamide is a very strong base and removes both molecules of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) from the vicinal dibromide, giving an alkyne.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CHBr-CH_3} \xrightarrow{2\,\mathrm{NaNH_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-C} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{C-CH_3} + 2\,\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_3}\)

**C = but-2-yne**, \(\mathrm{CH_3-C} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{C-CH_3}\)

[Note: the first step is taught in this chapter; the double dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide to an alkyne comes from the hydrocarbons chapter of the Std XI textbook.]

**A.** Phosphorus tribromide replaces the hydroxyl group of the alcohol by bromine (section 10.3.1, method b):

\(3\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} + \mathrm{PBr_3} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 3\,\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)

**A = 2-bromopropane**, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3}\)

**B.** Ammonia acts as the nucleophile and displaces bromide (Table 10.3, entry 4). Excess ammonia is used so that the reaction stops at the primary amine instead of going on to the secondary and tertiary amines:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3} + \mathrm{NH_3\ (excess)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(NH_2)-CH_3} + \mathrm{HBr}\)

**B = propan-2-amine** (isopropylamine), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-NH_2}\)

In the structure shown the halogen is attached **directly to a carbon of the carbon-carbon double bond**, that is, to an \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon.

By the classification of section 10.1.1 this makes it a **vinyl halide**.

(For contrast: if the halogen were on the \(sp^3\) carbon next to the double bond it would be an allyl halide, and if it were on a carbon of a benzene ring it would be an aryl halide.)

The two structures drawn are resonance structures: one of the lone pairs on the halogen is delocalised into the \(\pi\)-bond, and in the second structure the carbon-halogen bond is drawn as a **double** bond.

The real molecule is a resonance hybrid, so the C-X bond has **partial double bond character**. A double bond is shorter than a single bond, so the C-X bond in a vinyl halide is **shorter and stronger** than the C-X bond of an alkyl halide, where the halogen is on an \(sp^3\) carbon and no such delocalisation is possible.

The \(sp^2\) hybridisation of the carbon works the same way: an \(sp^2\) carbon is more electronegative than an \(sp^3\) carbon and holds the bonding electrons more tightly, shortening the bond further.

The chapter gives the corresponding figures for the closely similar case of a haloarene: the C-Cl bond is **169 pm** in chlorobenzene against **178 pm** in an alkyl chloride.

**No, a vinyl halide does not react by the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism.**

Justification. The slow, rate-determining step of an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction is heterolysis of the C-X bond to give a carbocation. Two things stop that happening here.

**i.** As the resonance shown makes clear, the C-X bond has partial double bond character and is therefore short and strong, so it does not break readily.

**ii.** The cation that would be left behind is a **vinyl cation**, whose empty orbital lies in the plane of the molecule and cannot overlap with the \(\pi\)-bond. It gains no resonance stabilisation, so it is a very high energy species and is not formed.

This is the same pair of arguments the chapter uses for haloarenes, where the phenyl cation produced by self-ionisation is likewise not stabilised by resonance. (The \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) route is closed too, because backside attack on the planar \(sp^2\) carbon is hindered by the \(\pi\)-electron cloud of the double bond.)
